title: Detect an independently verifiable extraterrestrial technology

concept.text: The innovation would be an independently verifiable discovery of a signal or artifact made by technology of extraterrestrial origin. A technosignature is evidence of technology: detecting one need not involve receiving an intentional message, decoding information or contacting its makers. Breakthrough Listen’s stated search for signs of extraterrestrial technology provides a concrete example of this scientific goal.

Conceptual clarification: the essential requirement is extraterrestrial technological provenance. Showing that something is located beyond Earth would not suffice, because human spacecraft and transmissions also operate in space. A convincing discovery would need evidence that the phenomenon is technological and that its origin cannot credibly be attributed to human activity. The concept includes possible signals and artifacts beyond the radio candidates illustrated by the supplied source.

significance.text: Conditional scientific implication: a verified discovery would establish that technology arose beyond Earth. It would turn the existence of extraterrestrial technology from an open possibility into an observational result, giving astronomy and research on life and intelligence a new empirical starting point. The significance follows from what the proposed discovery would establish; the supplied evidence does not report that this discovery has occurred.

Conditional downstream possibilities would depend on the evidence available. A well-localized source could motivate targeted observations of its environment, while a sufficiently informative signal or artifact might permit investigation of its operation, history or makers. Those possibilities are additional research opportunities, not guaranteed consequences. A detection would not by itself establish that the makers still exist, that the technology remains active, that it represents a whole civilization or that communication is feasible. Evidence of technology also would not automatically establish life on a particular exoplanet.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a convincing attribution of an observed phenomenon to extraterrestrial technology, with enough accessible evidence for independent investigators to check that conclusion. The Proxima Centauri candidate illustrates one central obstacle: apparent association with an astronomical target can survive initial filtering and still be explained by human interference. The supplied release describes checks involving neighboring observations and possible satellite sources, showing why observing in a target’s direction is only an initial clue.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: investigators must connect several distinct findings—where the phenomenon originates, whether the recorded feature is real, whether it requires a technological explanation and whether human technology can account for it. Instrument behavior, calibration errors, intermittent interference and natural astrophysical processes can undermine different parts of that chain. Independent observations must preserve the relevant feature while avoiding shared instrumental or analytical mistakes. For a transient event or a faint artifact, obtaining enough additional evidence may itself be the limiting barrier.

Methodological synthesis: there is no single radio-signal test that can establish the provenance of every possible technosignature. Evidence appropriate to a transmission may differ from evidence appropriate to a physical artifact or another astronomical anomaly. An unexplained feature alone would leave a gap between failing to identify its cause and positively establishing extraterrestrial technology. The required breakthrough includes closing that gap with converging evidence, while acknowledging which alternatives remain viable.

current_state.text: In its release dated 25 October 2021, Breakthrough Initiatives reported the analysis of an intriguing Breakthrough Listen candidate observed in the direction of Proxima Centauri. The analysis suggested that the signal was unlikely to originate in that system and instead favored interference from Earth-based human technology. The particular interference source remained unidentified. That residual uncertainty does not erase the evidence favoring interference, but it means the account should not be described as having conclusively identified the responsible device.

The demonstrated achievement in this example is the investigation and rejection of a promising candidate as evidence for technology in the Proxima Centauri system. It illustrates the difficulty of separating a target-associated radio signal from interference; it does not establish how all possible technosignatures would behave or how they should be tested. The release documents a relevant search and false-positive analysis, not a successful detection of extraterrestrial technology.

Evidence scope: the supplied review assessed a complete, untruncated copy of the news release, with no extraction issues recorded. It did not assess the full underlying research papers. The dated account therefore supports the reported 2021 conclusion at the level of the release, without providing a paper-level assessment here. The supplied freshness record is empty, so these materials cannot establish the field’s status through 1 November 2026 or subsequent developments. The source’s recorded retrieval on 11 November 2026 does not make its scientific account more recent than 2021.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent observations would establish an astronomical origin and reproduce, or independently corroborate, a feature whose technological explanation is compelling after credible human, instrumental and natural alternatives have been tested. Establishing an astronomical location would be one component of the case; the evidence would also need to establish extraterrestrial technological provenance. A readable message would not be required. These are proposed criteria for this record, not an established protocol prescribed by the supplied release.
completion_criteria.label: Independent observations establish astronomical origin and extraterrestrial technological provenance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: investigators should make the relevant observations, calibration information, processing methods and alternative-explanation tests available for independent scrutiny. Where feasible, separate instruments, observatories and analysis teams should recover the decisive evidence. For a nonrepeating event, independent corroboration or additional physical evidence would need to compensate for the inability to observe the same event again; a single unexplained recording would leave a substantial verification gap.
completion_criteria.label: Disclosed evidence and methods enable independent reproduction or corroboration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: a convincing case should state what has been established about the source, the technological feature and the remaining uncertainties. No numerical confidence threshold is supplied or adopted here. Finite observations can establish the demonstrated breadth of checks and the strength of a particular attribution; they cannot exhaust every imaginable natural or human explanation. Completion would concern a compelling, reproducible discovery of at least one extraterrestrial technology, without implying that every future candidate could be classified or that its makers could be contacted.
completion_criteria.label: Source attribution states established technological evidence and remaining uncertainties

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: AST-01, “Establish that an exoplanet hosts life,” is the closest overlap because extraterrestrial technology would bear directly on research into life and intelligence. The evidentiary targets remain distinct. Evidence of life need not indicate technology, while a technological signal or artifact need not establish that a particular exoplanet currently hosts life. Its makers could be elsewhere, no longer living or separated from the observed evidence by a long interval.

Roster-based synthesis: AST-08, “Produce resolved surface maps of rocky exoplanets,” could supply environmental context or spatial information useful in investigating a candidate associated with a planet. A resolved map would not automatically reveal technology, and AST-02 does not require a planetary surface map. Each concept retains its own completion requirement.

Roster-based synthesis: AST-09, “Make neutrino astronomy capable of routinely resolving hidden cosmic sources,” and AST-10, “Open the millihertz gravitational-wave sky as a working observatory,” overlap methodologically through source localization, instrument validation and separation of signals from backgrounds. Their goals concern observational capabilities for cosmic sources; neither capability would itself establish extraterrestrial technology. AST-02 is defined by the provenance and interpretation of the discovery rather than by opening a particular observing channel.

Roster-based synthesis: AST-03 through AST-07 and AST-11 through AST-14 address other physical constituents, cosmic histories, backgrounds or astrophysical mechanisms. Their relevant connection is the shared need to distinguish a new interpretation from instrumental effects and competing physical explanations. The supplied materials establish no specific dependency between those discoveries and AST-02, so they remain separate innovations.

unresolved_issues: The supplied materials do not establish whether later work changed the interpretation of this candidate or produced other relevant detections through November 2026.
The specific terrestrial interference source favored in the Proxima Centauri candidate analysis remained unidentified in the supplied account.
The underlying research papers were not assessed in the supplied review, leaving their detailed methods and evidentiary strength outside this record’s verified scope.
The appropriate verification tests would depend on the kind of signal or artifact discovered; the supplied materials do not establish a universal protocol or numerical acceptance threshold.

brief.title: Verifiable discovery of technology made beyond Earth
possible: People could point to a signal or object and establish that technology arose beyond Earth. Independent researchers could check the discovery. It would not require a readable message or contact with its makers.
A source with a known location could become a target for further observations. An informative signal or object could let researchers investigate how it worked, its history or its makers.
why: Whether technology exists beyond Earth would become a question with an observed answer. Astronomers and researchers studying life and intelligence would gain a new starting point grounded in something they could examine.

sources.showed: The team investigated a promising radio signal seen toward Proxima Centauri. Its analysis favored interference from human technology, although the responsible device remained unknown.
sources.quote: Taken together, this evidence suggests that the signal is interference from human technology, although we were unable to identify its specific source.
sources.cited_for: A signal can pass initial checks for a distant source and still come from human technology.
sources.not_established: The analysis did not establish technology of extraterrestrial origin.

sources.showed: The researchers traced the signal called blc1 to interacting local sources of radio interference. They found similar signals linked to frequencies used by electronic devices.
sources.quote:
We ﬁnd dozens of instances of radio interference with similar morphologies to blc1 at
frequencies harmonically related to common clock oscillators.
sources.cited_for: Detailed follow-up can expose human interference that resembles a signal from distant technology.
sources.not_established: Rejecting this candidate does not establish a test that works for every possible extraterrestrial signal or object.

sources.showed: The team used LOFAR radio telescope stations in Ireland and Sweden simultaneously. Comparing their observations helped reject human interference.
sources.quote:
As a
result, this narrowband signal is rejected as a genuine
sky-bound signal.
sources.cited_for: Observations from separate sites can test whether a signal truly comes from the sky.
sources.not_established: The search did not establish an extraterrestrial technological source.

sources.showed: Software trained to recognize signal patterns found eight promising radio signals for further observation.
sources.quote:
returning 8 promising
ETI signals of interest for re-observation as part of the Breakthrough Listen initiative.
sources.cited_for: Pattern-learning software can find candidates that earlier searches missed.
sources.not_established: Promising candidates still require evidence that excludes human interference and establishes their origin.

sources.showed: The team searched for brief flashes of light and found no evidence of extraterrestrial technology. Detecting pulses from a human satellite's laser tested the search method.
sources.quote: did not reveal any signals consistent with a technosignature.
sources.cited_for: Laser pulses from a known source can test a search for artificial light from beyond Earth.
sources.not_established: Detecting a human satellite's laser does not demonstrate detection of extraterrestrial technology.

shown: Breakthrough Listen and its collaborators have developed ways to find promising signals and challenge their apparent origins. Their work includes rejecting a deceptive radio candidate, comparing observations across distant sites, finding candidates with learning software and testing searches for brief light pulses.
missing: A signal or object still needs a compelling technological explanation whose origin cannot credibly be attributed to humans.
Independent observations must preserve the decisive feature while excluding shared instrument or analysis errors.
Other researchers need enough observations and methods to reproduce or independently support the discovery.

milestones.label: Independent observations establish technology of extraterrestrial origin
milestones.explanation: Independent observations would have to establish an astronomical origin and compelling evidence of technology after testing human, instrumental and natural explanations. This would establish who could not credibly have made it.

milestones.label: Shared evidence lets independent researchers confirm the result
milestones.explanation: Shared observations and methods would have to let others reproduce or independently support the decisive finding. This would let the discovery withstand scrutiny beyond the original team.

milestones.label: Source attribution separates established findings from remaining uncertainty
milestones.explanation: The case would have to state what is established about the source and its technology, alongside remaining uncertainties. This would define the discovery's reach without implying that contact is possible.

uncertain: The right verification tests depend on whether the discovery is a transmission, a physical object or another phenomenon.
No universal numerical threshold defines when the combined evidence becomes convincing.
A discovery would not by itself establish whether its makers still exist or whether their technology remains active.

page.title: Detection of extraterrestrial technosignatures
page.definition: A technosignature is observable evidence of technology. Detection is complete when investigators confirm that extraterrestrial beings built or used the technology responsible for an observation. The evidence could be a transmission, an artifact or an effect of engineering, such as waste heat from a structure that intercepts starlight. Confirmation requires neither decoding a message nor contacting its makers.

goal.need: Earth is the only world known to have produced technological life. Even finding microbes elsewhere would leave open whether other life ever developed technology. Surveys can limit how common particular technologies are within their reach. One confirmed example would establish that another technological intelligence had existed. A nearby artifact could be studied in detail, while a distant signal might reveal little more than its makers’ existence at the time of transmission.

figures.caption: Optical-pulse searches reported by VERITAS in 2023
figures.note: These are search results, not limits applicable to every possible optical transmitter.

statements.body: Breakthrough Initiatives identifies the search for extraterrestrial technological evidence as the purpose of Breakthrough Listen.
statements.quote: an astronomical science program searching for technosignatures – signs of technology that may have been developed by extraterrestrial intelligence.

statements.body: Participants in the NASA Technosignatures Workshop identify the scientific inference that motivates the search.
statements.quote:
Technosignatures represent any sign of technology that we can use to infer the
existence of intelligent life elsewhere in the universe
statements.context: This is the workshop participants’ report, rather than an adopted NASA discovery standard.

statements.body: The National Research Council’s Astronomy Survey Committee recommended a sustained astronomical search for extraterrestrial intelligence.
statements.quote: an astronomical Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence be initiated as a long-term effort.
statements.context: The committee recommended modest support and judged the chance of a detection during the following decade uncertain and possibly small.

completion.title: Investigators confirm extraterrestrial technological origin in a peer-reviewed verification report.
completion.criterion: The discoverers work with other investigators to authenticate and substantiate the detection. The other investigators involved concur that the evidence is due to extraterrestrial intelligence, with a degree of certainty the discoverers judge credible. Ideally, multiple facilities and more than one organisation examine the evidence independently with different instruments and methods. The verification report undergoes peer review and includes the underlying data, analysis process, verification results, conclusions, interpretations and any detected information content.
completion.set_by: International Academy of Astronautics, Declaration of Principles Concerning the Conduct of the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence, 2026 update, Principles 1 and 3.
completion.threshold_quote: a degree of certainty judged by the discoverers to be credible
completion.basis: Principle 3 explicitly distinguishes confirmed extraterrestrial evidence from candidate evidence and calls for a peer-reviewed verification report. It supplies a qualitative scientific acceptance test, without prescribing a probability or significance level. The declaration’s definition includes transmissions, astronomical effects of technology and artifacts.

milestones.title: A technosignature search records a signal above its predefined noise threshold.
milestones.criterion: A search records a signal in observational data above the noise threshold specified for that experiment.
milestones.set_by: Forgan et al., Rio 2.0, Terminology; proposed SETI verification framework.

milestones.title: At least one additional measurement with independent instrumentation confirms the same phenomenon.
milestones.criterion: Independent instrumentation records at least one additional measurement confirming the same phenomenon, satisfying Rio class V. An instrumental explanation can still be consistent with the measurements.
milestones.set_by: Forgan et al., Rio 2.0, Terminology; proposed SETI verification framework.
milestones.threshold_quote: one extra measurement with independent instrumentation

milestones.title: A verified candidate phenomenon is shown to have a non-instrumental origin.
milestones.criterion: For a signal already verified by independent instrumentation, the evidence rules out instrumental effects as its cause. This establishes Rio class C, candidate. Natural sources and human activity remain possible explanations.
milestones.set_by: Forgan et al., Rio 2.0, Terminology; proposed SETI verification framework.
milestones.threshold_quote: demonstrably not due to instrumentation effects

milestones.title: A candidate requires extraterrestrial design after natural and human explanations are excluded.
milestones.criterion: A broad community of experts concludes that the phenomenon requires extraterrestrial design and engineering. Rio 2.0 question C2 assigns 8 when only an artificial extraterrestrial explanation fits and 9 for clearly designed information or an obviously artificial alien artifact available for close inspection. A phenomenon unexplained by known natural or human causes alone earns 6.
milestones.set_by: Forgan et al., Rio 2.0, question C2; proposed SETI assessment framework.
milestones.threshold_quote: Only extraterrestrial, artificial explanations make sense

milestones.title: An optical pulse detector registers a test flash in both channels at once.
milestones.criterion: In the Agassiz Station optical pulse test, a fiber-coupled light-emitting diode supplies a flash before each observation. Both detector channels must cross their lowest thresholds simultaneously. The recorded pulses must overlap in time and their amplitudes must agree within one discriminator level.
milestones.set_by: Harvard-Smithsonian targeted optical SETI search, Agassiz Station two-channel photometer protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: the lowest thresholds are simultaneously exceeded in both channels.

milestones.title: At least two research groups analyze signal data from a single instrument.
milestones.criterion: More than one research group analyzes the signal data, ideally using different methods. At this stage only one set of instruments has detected the signal. Rio 2.0 calls this class U, unverified.
milestones.set_by: Forgan et al., Rio 2.0, proposed terminology for unverified signals.
milestones.threshold_quote: data have been analysed by more than one research group

not_found: No universal numerical discovery threshold was found in the IAA declarations, Rio 2.0 framework or Breakthrough Listen verification checklist.
No laboratory validation threshold applicable to every technosignature class was found.

results.finding: One narrow-band radio signal persisted across five hours of Parkes observations of Proxima Centauri.
results.detail: The release describes Doppler drift and target-pointing filters. Neither establishes the experiment’s noise threshold.
results.quote: A narrow-band, Doppler-drifting signal, persisting over five hours of observations, that appears to be present only in “ON” observations of the target star and not in the interspersed “OFF” observations, had some of the characteristics expected from a technosignature candidate.

results.finding: For one Parkes candidate, the Breakthrough Listen follow-up found around 60 similar signals that also appeared off target.
results.detail: The release describes two papers with different lead authors and identifies both analyses with the same research team.
results.quote: She found around 60 signals that share many characteristics of the candidate, but are also seen in their respective OFF observations.

results.finding: The Parkes search detected blc1 at SNR > 10 in five observations toward Proxima Centauri.
results.detail: Table 1 gives a mean SNR of 17.956. The analysis attributes the signal to local radio-frequency interference.
results.quote:
We determined that the
original signal on 2019 April 29 (blc1) appeared at signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) > 10 in ﬁve observations.

results.finding: Eight Parkes follow-up sessions yielded zero redetections of blc1.
results.detail: The archival lookalikes came from the original receiver. The paper discusses simultaneous observations with MeerKAT as future work.
results.quote:
No signals of any drift rate were detected at
νblc1 ± 2 kHz in any of these re-observations.

results.finding: Three interference lookalikes linked blc1 to mixing involving an approximately 2 MHz clock oscillator.
results.detail: The lookalikes spanned all three digitizer cards, which weighs against a spurious signal generated in the receiver’s digital systems.
results.quote:
In the bottom panel of Figure 5, we see these exact spacings relating
blc1 (within propagated error, of order 100 Hz) with three lookalikes at ∼ 712 MHz, ∼ 856 MHz, and ∼ 1062 MHz.

results.finding: The authors’ Rio 2.0 assessment of one radio signal of interest, blc1, yielded a final Rio score of 0.
results.detail: The reported zero is the overall Rio score. The authors separately report an aggregate C value of 1.
results.quote:
However, δ, the likelihood that this signal has an interstellar origin,
is 0.00001, leading to a ﬁnal Rio Score score of R = Q× δ = 0.

rejections, no signals of interest were identified among
the observed candidates.

results.finding: Of 5,137 sources with Dyson-sphere-like spectra, 368 passed the WISE mid-infrared signal-to-noise cut in both bands.
results.detail: The authors applied the cut after an initial visual inspection showed that many low-SNR catalog detections were unreliable. A second inspection screened the sources above the cut for blends, irregular structure and nebulosity.
results.quote: We selected sources with SNR higher than 3.5 in both the W3 and W4 bands, resulting in 368 sources.

results.finding: Among seven infrared-excess candidates checked for WISE source confusion, one showed a suspicious positional offset.
results.detail: The offset occurred between WISE W1 and W3 for candidate G. A closely aligned background source remains possible even for candidates without a significant offset.

results.finding: For one Dyson sphere candidate, the excess in two mid-infrared bands aligns with a background active galactic nucleus.
results.detail: The supplied arXiv version states that MNRAS Letters accepted the paper, which supports confirmed status. The supplied document is the arXiv version.
results.quote: While the W1 and W2 infrared bands align closely with the M-dwarf star, the W3 and W4 bands are offset towards the AGN (J2335-0004), indicating that the latter dominates the mid-infrared emission.

results.finding: JWST/MIRI independently recovered the WISE mid-infrared emission in both targets (n=2) and resolved the dominant emitters about 1 arcsec from the stars.
results.detail: The MIRI-derived and WISE fluxes differ in some bands, most prominently by about 4σ in W4 for E. The independent observations corroborate the emission and resolve its source.
results.quote: From these images, we conclude that the excess mid-IR flux seen in WISE data for Dyson-sphere candidates D and E can be attributed to contamination by mid-IR bright background galaxies that appear blended with the M-dwarf stars when observed at the angular resolution of WISE.

results.finding: For both Dyson-sphere targets (n=2), galaxies about 1 arcsec from the stars explain the apparent stellar mid-infrared excess.
results.detail: MIRI spectroscopy places the galaxies at redshifts of about 0.922 for D and 0.4104 for E. The source presents the galaxy attribution as a new analysis in this preprint.
results.quote: The JWST/MIRI imaging alone rules out both the Dyson-sphere and extreme debris-disk explanations for the mid-IR excess of candidates D and E, since both of these scenarios would predict the mid-IR radiation to originate at distances too close to the M dwarfs to be resolvable in MIRI imaging.

results.finding: Agassiz Station LED flashes before 15,897 observations passed the two-channel test, including amplitude agreement within one discriminator level, with rare exceptions.
results.detail: The paper gives the observation count and describes test failures as rare. It gives no exact pass or failure count.
results.quote:
the LED test ﬂashes, which are
done before every observation, pass this test with only rare
exceptions.

results.finding: Harvard’s nanosecond optical pulse search recorded 4,746 above-threshold triggers in 15,897 stellar observations.
results.detail: The 274 events remaining after exclusion of nights with anomalously high trigger rates were consistent with a uniform background rate. The only plausible Harvard–Princeton trigger pair failed the event checks at both sites.
results.quote:
In the ﬁve years of observations, we recorded 4746 ‘‘trig-
gers’’ (i.e., instances when the lowest thresholds are simul-
taneously exceeded in both channels).

results.finding: The HARPS search for continuous-wave laser emissions flagged 285 above-threshold spectral spikes in spectra from 2,821 stars.
results.detail: Three candidates remained unexplained after follow-up screening. Natural stellar emission remained a possible explanation.
results.quote: Our Tier 1 automated search, based on the above criteria (4-60 pixels in a row above threshold, with several known bright airglow lines excluded) yielded 285 “spike” candidates from our 2,821 stars.

results.finding: Among 4,898,812 main-sequence FGK stars, 53 mid-infrared excess candidates passed the search cuts.
results.detail: The fitted excess luminosities were consistent with extreme debris disks and possible planetary collisions.
results.quote: We obtained a set of 53 candidates that display interesting (M)IR excess.

results.finding: An automated search of 224,168 ZTF images recorded 16,693 bright, isolated, uncatalogued detections near Earth’s shadow center.
results.detail: The count is from Sample B, subset III, which also required separation from catalogued sources and nearby unmatched detections. It counts detections rather than distinct objects.

results.finding: In a three-field Small Magellanic Cloud survey, Mopra independently re-detected 3 Parkes radio candidates.
results.detail: The follow-up required the differential Doppler shift expected of a sidereal source. Subsequent on-source and off-source observations ruled out all three as extraterrestrial candidates.
results.quote:
Such “extraterrestrial candidates” were found in non-
interference bands three times during this search.

results.finding: Two research groups analyzed data for one Wow! Signal event recorded by Big Ear.
results.detail: The later team corrected the channel ordering assumed in the original analysis. The signal’s origin remains unresolved.
results.quote: This study offers the first comprehensive reanalysis of the original Ohio SETI data at the time of the Wow! Signal detection.

results.finding: Two research groups analyzed the same SDSS spectrum of one candidate star flagged for possible optical pulses.
results.detail: The verdict applies to analysis of the SDSS candidate. The APF follow-up yielded no detection, and Hippke interpreted the SDSS peak as a processing effect caused by absorption-line spacing.
results.quote:
As a crosscheck, I have also re-reduced the SDSS spec-
trum of one of the stars for which Borra & Trottier
(2016) found a signal (SDSS J160133.35+273355.2, Fig-
ure 2 (b)).

results.finding: Two research groups analyzed Kepler dimming data for one star, KIC 8462852, a candidate for megastructure occultations.
results.quote:

definition = "A technosignature is observable evidence of technology. Detection is complete when investigators confirm that extraterrestrial beings built or used the technology responsible for an observation. The evidence could be a transmission, an artifact or an effect of engineering, such as waste heat from a structure that intercepts starlight. Confirmation requires neither decoding a message nor contacting its makers.". Reason: The definition needs an example of how an observation can reveal engineering without a message or direct observation of the artifact.

goal.need = "Earth is the only world known to have produced technological life. Even finding microbes elsewhere would leave open whether other life ever developed technology. Surveys can limit how common particular technologies are within their reach. One confirmed example would establish that another technological intelligence had existed. A nearby artifact could be studied in detail, while a distant signal might reveal little more than its makers\u2019 existence at the time of transmission.". Reason: The current rationale recounts two unsuccessful searches and omits the scientific question that a confirmed detection would settle.
